questions.question: How do you use when().thenReturn() to stub a method in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito when thenReturn | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`when(mock.method(args)).thenReturn(value)`** configures the mock to return `value` when `method(args)` is called. This is the core stubbing syntax. Call it in the Arrange phase of your test before invoking the class under test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core Mockito syntax — must know this cold
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting up the stub after calling the method under test — the stub must be configured before the act
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show chaining: thenReturn for multiple calls, thenThrow, and thenAnswer for dynamic responses

sections.title: Stub Before Act
sections.content: `when(userRepository.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(testUser))` — when the code calls `userRepository.findById(1L)`, it returns the test user. **Order matters**: stub in Arrange, call in Act. **Multiple returns**: `when(mock.method()).thenReturn(first, second, third)` — first call returns 'first', second returns 'second', subsequent calls return 'third'. **Throw**: `when(mock.method()).thenThrow(new RuntimeException("error"))`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- when(mock.method(args)).thenReturn(value)
- Must configure BEFORE the method under test is called
- Multiple returns: thenReturn(v1, v2, v3)
- Chain: .thenReturn(v).thenThrow(ex)
- thenAnswer: dynamic return based on invocation arguments
- Returns default for non-stubbed methods: null/0/false
- Argument matching: any(), eq(), specific values
- BDD alias: given(mock.method()).willReturn(value)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: when-thenReturn is the core Mockito stubbing syntax. I write when, then in parentheses the mock call I want to configure, then .thenReturn with the value it should return. This goes in the Arrange phase before I call the method under test. I can chain multiple returns for consecutive calls — thenReturn with multiple values, where the last value is returned for all subsequent calls. I can also chain thenThrow to throw an exception on a specific call. For dynamic return values that depend on the argument passed, I use thenAnswer with a lambda that receives the invocation and returns a computed value.

questions.question: How do you stub a method to throw an exception in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito thenThrow Exception | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use `when(mock.method()).thenThrow(new ExceptionClass("message"))` or `thenThrow(ExceptionClass.class)`.** For void methods, use `doThrow(new Exception()).when(mock).voidMethod()`. This tests error handling paths in your code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Exception scenario testing with Mockito — very common in service layer tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not testing the error path — only the happy path — which leaves exception handling logic untested
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combine with assertThrows: stub the dependency to throw, then assert the service propagates or wraps the exception correctly

sections.title: Test Error Paths
sections.content: `when(repository.save(any())).thenThrow(new DataAccessException("DB down"))` — test how the service handles a database failure. Combined with JUnit's `assertThrows`: `DataAccessException ex = assertThrows(DataAccessException.class, () -> service.createOrder(order))`. For void methods: `doThrow(new IOException()).when(fileService).write(any())`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- thenThrow(new Exception()): throw an instance
- thenThrow(ExceptionClass.class): throw new instance of that class
- Void methods: doThrow().when(mock).voidMethod()
- Chain: thenReturn(x).thenThrow(ex) for first-then-throw
- Test: stub dep to throw, assert service handles/propagates correctly
- Checked exceptions: mock method must declare throws
- RuntimeException: no declaration needed
- Combine with assertThrows to verify exception propagation

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To simulate a dependency throwing an exception, I use thenThrow in the stubbing chain. For a regular method I write when-thenThrow. For a void method I use the doThrow-when form. Then in the test assertion I use assertThrows to verify that the class under test either propagates the exception or throws its own domain exception. Testing error paths is just as important as the happy path — if the repository throws a database exception, I want to verify the service either handles it gracefully or wraps it in an appropriate application exception with a meaningful message.

questions.question: How do you use thenAnswer() for dynamic stubbing in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito thenAnswer Dynamic Stubbing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`thenAnswer(invocation -> ...)` provides dynamic responses based on the actual arguments passed.** Use it when the return value depends on the input: echo the argument back, compute a result, or return different things based on the input value. More powerful than `thenReturn` for complex scenarios.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using when().thenReturn() with multiple values when thenAnswer would more clearly express the logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete example: a save method that returns the passed entity with an ID — a very common test scenario

sections.title: Dynamic Return Values
sections.content: Common use case — simulate save returning the entity with a generated ID: `when(repo.save(any(User.class))).thenAnswer(invocation -> { User u = invocation.getArgument(0); u.setId(100L); return u; })`. The lambda receives an `InvocationOnMock` — use `invocation.getArgument(0)` to get the first argument. This is cleaner than maintaining a list of return values for each possible input.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- thenAnswer(invocation -> computedReturn)
- invocation.getArgument(0): first argument passed
- invocation.getArguments(): all arguments as array
- Use when: return value depends on argument value
- Use when: need to simulate DB save returning entity with ID
- Alternative: AdditionalAnswers.returnsFirstArg() — common utility
- More complex than thenReturn — use only when needed
- Lambda can capture test variables for state simulation

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: thenAnswer lets me write a lambda that dynamically computes the return value based on what was actually passed to the mock. The lambda receives an InvocationOnMock object from which I can extract the arguments with getArgument. A classic use case is simulating a repository save method that returns the entity with a generated ID — I get the passed entity from the invocation, set its ID, and return it. This is more realistic than thenReturn with a pre-built object because it responds to what was actually passed. I use it when thenReturn is too static to express the relationship between input and output.

questions.question: What happens when a non-stubbed method is called on a Mockito mock?
questions.title: Mockito Default Return Values | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Non-stubbed methods return safe default values: null for objects, 0 for numbers, false for booleans, empty collections for collection types.** This is the 'RETURNS_DEFAULTS' answer strategy. With strict stubbing, calling a non-stubbed method can indicate a test configuration problem.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting a NullPointerException when a non-stubbed method is called — mocks return safe defaults, not NPE
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Mockito has different default answer strategies: RETURNS_DEFAULTS, RETURNS_SMART_NULLS, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS

sections.title: Safe Defaults, Not Exceptions
sections.content: Mockito's default answer (RETURNS_DEFAULTS): null for object/String, 0 for int/long/double, false for boolean, empty collections for List/Set/Map. This means calling `mockList.size()` returns 0, `mockRepo.findById(1L)` returns null. **RETURNS_SMART_NULLS**: returns a SmartNull that throws NullPointerException with a helpful message when dereferenced — better for catching unstubbed chains. `Mockito.mock(Class.class, RETURNS_SMART_NULLS)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Default: null, 0, false, empty collections
- RETURNS_DEFAULTS: the standard safe defaults
- RETURNS_SMART_NULLS: null that gives helpful NPE message on dereference
- RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS: enables mock.getA().getB() — not recommended for new code
- CALLS_REAL_METHODS: like @Spy but as answer strategy
- Optional.empty() for Optional return types (Mockito 2+)
- Non-stubbed void methods: do nothing by default

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Non-stubbed methods on a Mockito mock return safe default values — null for object types, zero for numeric types, false for boolean, and empty collections for List, Set, and Map. This means tests don't immediately fail with NullPointerException just because a method wasn't stubbed. Mockito 2+ also returns Optional.empty() for Optional return types. If I want better error messages when non-stubbed methods are accidentally called, I can use RETURNS_SMART_NULLS as the mock's default answer strategy — it returns a special object that throws an informative NPE with the mock method call shown when you try to use the returned value.

questions.question: How do you stub void methods in Mockito?
questions.title: Stubbing Void Methods
questions.direct_answer: Use doNothing().when(mock).voidMethod() or doThrow().when(mock).voidMethod() because when().thenReturn() cannot be used with void return types.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the do*() API family, which is required for void methods and also safer for Spies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to use when(mock.voidMethod()).thenReturn(null) which does not compile for void methods
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention doAnswer() as the most flexible option when you need to execute custom logic when the void method is called

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
In Mockito, the when().thenReturn() pattern cannot be used for void methods because there is nothing to return — it will not even compile. Instead, Mockito provides the do*() family of methods that work differently: you specify what to do first, then chain .when(mock).method().

For void methods that should do nothing, which is actually the Mockito default, you can write doNothing().when(emailService).sendEmail(any()). This is useful when you want to be explicit that the method should be a no-op, or when you are using a Spy and want to suppress the real implementation.

For void methods that should throw an exception, use doThrow(new RuntimeException()).when(mock).voidMethod(). This is commonly used to test error handling paths.

For complex scenarios where you want to execute custom logic or capture arguments, doAnswer() is the most powerful option. You pass a lambda that receives the method arguments through an InvocationOnMock object and can execute any code you need.

A key point: the do*() style also works for non-void methods and is required when stubbing methods on a Spy to avoid accidentally calling the real method.

sections.title: Key Points
content: when().thenReturn() does not work for void methods — use doNothing() / doThrow() / doAnswer()
doNothing().when(mock).method() — suppresses the real call (default on mocks anyway)
doThrow(exception).when(mock).method() — makes the void method throw
doAnswer(invocation -> ...).when(mock).method() — for custom logic on void calls

questions.question: What is thenAnswer() and when do you use it?
questions.title: thenAnswer() in Mockito
questions.direct_answer: thenAnswer() lets you compute a dynamic return value based on the actual arguments passed to the stubbed method, unlike thenReturn() which always returns a static value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know when static stubbing is insufficient and how to provide argument-dependent responses
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using thenReturn() with a hardcoded value when the correct response depends on what input was passed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the lambda form: thenAnswer(inv -> inv.getArgument(0).toString().toUpperCase()) as a concrete example

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
thenReturn() is great when the stubbed method should always return the same value regardless of its input. But sometimes the correct response depends on what argument was passed, and that is where thenAnswer() comes in.

thenAnswer() accepts an Answer functional interface, so in modern Java you pass a lambda. The lambda receives an InvocationOnMock object, from which you can retrieve the actual arguments that were passed with getArgument(index). You then compute and return whatever value makes sense.

For example, if you have a repository method findById(Long id) and you want the mock to return a User whose id matches what was passed in, you would write: when(userRepo.findById(anyLong())).thenAnswer(inv -> Optional.of(new User(inv.getArgument(0)))).

Another common use case is simulating a save method that returns the saved object with an assigned ID — you can retrieve the argument, modify it, and return it from the lambda.

The tradeoff is complexity. thenAnswer() makes your test harder to read than thenReturn(). Use it only when the dynamic behavior is genuinely important to the test. If you find yourself writing very complex thenAnswer() lambdas, consider whether a Fake object would be a cleaner solution.

sections.title: Key Points
content: thenAnswer(inv -> ...) computes a return value dynamically based on arguments
Access method arguments via inv.getArgument(0), inv.getArgument(1), etc.
Use when thenReturn()'s static value is not sufficient for the test scenario
For very complex logic, consider a Fake object instead of a complex thenAnswer() lambda

questions.question: How do you stub the same method to return different values on consecutive calls?
questions.title: Consecutive Call Stubbing
questions.direct_answer: Chain multiple thenReturn() values or use thenReturn(val1, val2, val3); after the last value, all subsequent calls return the last one.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Mockito stubbing knowledge for stateful or retry scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling when().thenReturn() twice on the same method — only the last stubbing takes effect
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the pattern for simulating a retry: first call throws an exception, second call returns a value

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Sometimes you need a method to behave differently on successive calls — for example, simulating a retry where the first call fails and the second succeeds, or an iterator-like method that returns different data each time.

Mockito supports this with consecutive stubbing. The most readable way is to chain calls: when(mock.method()).thenReturn(firstValue).thenReturn(secondValue). You can also pass multiple values as varargs: when(mock.method()).thenReturn(first, second, third). After the stubbed sequence is exhausted, all subsequent calls return the last value.

You can mix thenReturn and thenThrow in the same chain: when(mock.getStatus()).thenThrow(new RuntimeException("timeout")).thenReturn("OK"). This is extremely useful for testing retry logic — the first call simulates a network failure and the second simulates success.

An important pitfall: if you stub the same method twice in separate when() calls, the second stubbing completely overrides the first for all calls. This catches many developers off guard. If you want different behaviour per call, you must use the chained or varargs form in a single stubbing declaration.

For more complex sequences you can use thenAnswer() with a counter, but chained thenReturn is sufficient for most interview and real-world scenarios.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Chain thenReturn() calls or use varargs: thenReturn(v1, v2, v3).
Mix thenThrow and thenReturn in the same chain to simulate retry scenarios.
After the sequence ends, Mockito returns the last stubbed value.
Two separate when() stubbings on the same method override each other — use chaining instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between when().thenReturn() and doReturn().when() and when should you prefer one over the other?
questions.title: when/thenReturn vs doReturn/when
questions.direct_answer: when().thenReturn() actually calls the method during setup (safe for mocks), while doReturn().when() bypasses the real call (required for spies and void methods).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's two stubbing APIs and their subtle but important difference
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using when().thenReturn() on a spy where the real method has side effects during the stubbing call itself
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly explain why the real method is invoked in when() stubbing for spies and why doReturn avoids this

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Both when().thenReturn() and doReturn().when() achieve the same goal — stubbing a method to return a value — but they differ in how Mockito intercepts the call during setup.

With when(mock.someMethod()).thenReturn(value), Mockito actually invokes someMethod() during the setup line to capture which method is being stubbed. For a full mock this is fine because the method is intercepted immediately and returns a default value. But for a spy, the real method runs before Mockito can intercept it. This means if the real method has side effects — like calling a database or throwing a NullPointerException because an internal field is not set up yet — the test blows up during setup, not during the actual test.

doReturn(value).when(spy).someMethod() takes the opposite approach: Mockito registers the stubbing without ever invoking the real method. This is why doReturn().when() is the correct choice for spies whenever you want to override a method without triggering its real implementation.

doReturn().when() is also the only option for void methods, because you cannot write when(mock.voidMethod()) — it does not compile because there is no return value to pass to when(). For void methods you use doNothing().when() or doThrow().when() instead.

As a practical rule: use when().thenReturn() by default for regular mocks, and switch to doReturn().when() for spies or void methods.

sections.title: Key Points
content: when().thenReturn(): invokes the method during setup — safe for mocks, dangerous for spies.
doReturn().when(): skips the real method entirely — required for spies and void methods.
Use doNothing().when(spy).method() for void methods on spies.
Rule of thumb: default to when/thenReturn for mocks; switch to doReturn/when for spies.
